title: The magic behind Portable Surrounds
summary: Read more about the unique combination of software and hardware that powers the Sonos ecosystem. Welcome to our technology blog.
body_markdown:
Many customers want the option of a more immersive, discrete surround sound experience — without permanently dedicating extra speakers, floor space, or power outlets to rear channels. At the same time, they want their home theater speakers to pull double duty: taken out of the surround setup and brought to another room, the patio, or on a trip, whenever they're not watching TV.


Sonos Portable Surrounds makes both directions effortless. Bring your portable speakers into the home theater room, set them behind the sofa, and you have a full surround sound experience. Pull one back out and it's instantly a standalone portable speaker again, ready for wherever you're headed next. That's the Portable Surrounds experience — portables becoming surrounds, and surrounds becoming portables, on demand.


Behind that simplicity is a mountain of innovation. Moving a speaker between roles in real time requires tight coordination between soundbar and portables, advanced networking and audio routing behaviours, and sensing strategies for devices being moved.


The three main technical pillars are:


-


Sonos Positioning Technology (SPT) that uses precision acoustic measurements to accurately place the portable speakers in the appropriate surround role.


-


A fully reworked accelerometer interface so that the portable speakers can respond to your movement in near real time.


-


A ground-up rebuild of how a Sonos speaker transitions in and out of the home theater surround roles quickly and reliably.


This blog will focus on the first of these, Sonos Positioning Technology as the building block that provides the system wide knowledge of the spatial relationship between the soundbar and the portable speakers. SPT not only recognizes when the portable speakers have been placed in the same room as the soundbar, but it also measures the angular position of each portable speaker in order to assign the left and right surround roles accurately.


Let’s dive in.


*Figure 1: Three pillars work together to place a portable speaker*


## Sonos Positioning Technology (SPT)


Sonos has utilized acoustic proximity detection for some time now. Both[Secure Setup and Roam Sound Swap have been utilizing near-ultrasonic (NUS) signals to infer proximity](https://tech-blog.sonos.com/posts/how-near-ultrasonic-audio-adds-spatial-awareness-to-the-sonos-system/) as NUS generally does not transit room boundaries. One of the main difficulties driving portable surrounds is that sensing speaker proximity is not enough. A specific role in the surround sound system needs to be assigned to each speaker, and this is where precise acoustic measurements come into play. To meet this need Sonos Positioning Technology (SPT) was developed.


*Figure 2: The listener places two portable speakers where is convenient — SPT works out each one’s angle relative to the soundbar to assign it as left or right surround*


When an enrolled portable speaker is placed somewhere in your house, Sonos Fabric will coordinate across the system to enable SPT. The microphones on the soundbar will be turned on and then the participating portable speakers will take turns playing back near-ultrasonic signals. The number of signals emitted by each speaker depends on many factors as the system will dynamically assess proximity, position, and confidence metrics.


*Figure 3: From “is it here?” to "which channel should it play?”*


The fundamental physics underlying all of this means that the microphones on the soundbar will “hear” the chirp emitted at different times depending on how close they are to the portable speaker as demonstrated in the animation below.


*Figure 4: How a microphone array senses direction*


With a known microphone geometry on our soundbars the problem then reduces to:


-


Reliably detecting the precise time at which the sound showed up at one microphone versus all the others


-


Inferring the angle from which the sound must have come to have generated the detected timing signature.


The specific geometry of the microphone array dictates exactly how each of the preceding problems are approached. SPT has been tuned to work across many different soundbars with varying microphone placements and a discussion of some of the issues follows.


In the microphone time of arrival animation above one of the difficulties of the larger soundbars is shown. In many situations the soundsource is considered to be much further away from the soundbar compared to the separation of the microphones on the soundbar. We are then able to make a “plane-wave” approximation. The animation above depicts the true situation when the sound-source is not distant enough to make this approximation, the wavefronts look circular and to get the most accurate translation from the relative times-of-arrival at the microphones into an incoming angle, we use a non-linear least squares optimizer to find the best fit location for the soundsource. One example of this non-linear process is demonstrated in the animation below.


*Figure 5: An animation of 5 non-linear least squares iterations to estimate the true position of a sound source*


Our more compact soundbars fall into a different category because the microphones were placed on a smaller scale, so we are able to make the plane-wave approximation. This allows us to run a linear least squares solution which is computationally efficient. However, in practice the tradeoff in the required accuracy of the arrival time-stamping means that the angle estimation performance is much more sensitive to multi-path interference and noise.


Therefore the level of reverberance and the separation of the microphones determine how accurately we need to be able to time-stamp the arrival at each microphone. One of the important properties of the signals we use is that in a reverberant environment the impulse response (IR) we estimate\[1\] based on mismatched filtering becomes a series of time-delayed and scaled copies of the anechoic impulse response and the largest driver of how accurately we can timestamp becomes the bandwidth. In all figures and references we are plotting the envelope of the IR. We use the envelope to avoid any fast oscillations that might be in the signal (such as the carrier frequency).


*Figure 6: Signal bandwidth vs peak resolvability*


Plotted above is the theoretical anechoic IR of a signal of three different bandwidths, the width of the peak is inversely proportional to the bandwidth of the signal. With our larger soundbars we are able to operate with a 4 kHz sweep because the separation of the microphones means that the system is less sensitive to small timing errors.


In order to operate in real-world conditions with compact soundbars we needed to increase the bandwidth from 4kHz to 6kHz. This resolution buys less interference from the close-reflections that arrive a short time after the initial, direct path. In the figure above the significant sharpening of the peaks in the IR is highlighted. The tradeoff in this situation is audibility\[2\]. To compensate for this we use a modified signal that places less energy in the audible frequencies. The lower energy in the more audible regions then has to be inverted in our mismatched filter to recover the desired overall shaping.


*Figure 7: An example compact soundbar sweep*


In order to time-stamp accurately in a reverberant environment we take advantage of the guarantee that the most direct path sound takes will arrive first. The figure below highlights what the IR traces look like in a real room under different conditions. SPT estimates the most direct sound in this impulse response. For the messy non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions below you can see that this becomes much more difficult and we rely on various regularization mechanisms to find a set of peaks consistent with the microphone geometry when there is no first and obvious choice. As discussed later, this is one example of a cue that might affect the decision of whether or not the portable will be bonded as surround.


*Figure 8: SPT impulse responses line-of-sight comparison*


When looking for a “first arrival” peak one of the classic problems is leading sidelobes that can interfere with the first arrival estimation. To reduce this effect we apply spectral shaping (the mismatch in the mismatched filter) that optimizes the tradeoff between the widening of the mainlobe and suppression of the leading sidelobes. This shaping can be applied to the transmitted signal, the received signal, or some combination depending on background noise or audibility considerations. Demonstrated in the figure below is a marginal widening of the main peak for significant reduction in the sidelobes.


*Figure 9: Spectral shaping trade-off: square vs shaped window*


In addition to estimating the time-of-arrival, the impulse responses of the positioning signals provide a wealth of information about the nature and quality of the measurements. The steepness of the peaks, the spacing between peaks of interest, the amount of energy that slowly decays, can all be fed into machine-learning algorithms to better refine the speaker’s understanding of the environment.


*Figure 10: Bonding model features in impulse responses*


In particular, SPT attempts to understand the difference between a soundbar’s ability to “hear” the portable is present versus the portable being placed in a position where the user wants it to act as a satellite. This model continues development and will improve over time.


Sonos Fabric and portable surrounds have introduced the ability to magically create an immersive sound experience by automatically moving your portable devices into and out of the home theater environment. This is made possible by Sonos Positioning Technology, which works behind the scenes to make quiet acoustic measurements which determine precisely what role your portable speaker should play in your household.


### References


\[1\] Müller, S., & Massarani, P. (2001). Transfer Function Measurement with Sweeps. Journal of the Audio Engineering Society, 49(6), 443–471


[\[2\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261767650_Extended_high-frequency_9-20_kHz_audiometry_reference_thresholds_in_645_healthy_subjects) Rodríguez Valiente, A. et al. (2014) ‘Extended high-frequency (9–20 kHz) audiometry reference thresholds in 645 healthy subjects’, International Journal of Audiology, 53(8), pp. 531–545.
